The constructor removes unknown handler names by mutating `metricDef.getHandlers()` in-place. This violates `MetricDef`’s immutability contract (see its class javadoc) and can have surprising side effects if the same `MetricConfiguration` is reused elsewhere. Prefer filtering into a separate validated list/map inside `BeanFinder` (or during parsing/building of `MetricDef`) without mutating the `MetricDef` instance.

This issue also appears on line 194 of the same file.

`MetricDef` is documented as immutable, but it stores the provided `handlers` list directly. This is currently mutated by `BeanFinder` and also means callers can mutate `handlers` after construction. Consider defensively copying (e.g., `List.copyOf(...)`) and/or storing handler holders instead of mutable names to preserve immutability and avoid cross-thread surprises.

Changing `JmxTelemetry.start()` / `start(Supplier<...>)` to return `AutoCloseable` instead of `JmxTelemetry` is a source-breaking change for library consumers that previously relied on chaining or the return type. Consider keeping the old signature (possibly deprecated) and adding a new method that returns an `AutoCloseable` handle for stopping/cleanup, or otherwise provide a migration path to avoid an abrupt API break.

The returned `AutoCloseable` from `start()` runs `finder.shutdown()` and then `registrar.close()`. If `shutdown()` throws (e.g., `InterruptedException`), `registrar.close()` will be skipped, potentially leaking instruments. Consider ensuring `registrar.close()` runs in a `finally` block and preserving interrupt status when catching `InterruptedException`.

`close()` logs only `e.getMessage()` when an instrument fails to close, which drops the exception type/stack trace and makes debugging harder. Prefer logging the exception itself (e.g., pass `e` to the logger) and include enough context to identify which instrument failed.

This test method declares `throws Exception` but appears to only need narrower checked exceptions (or none). Per project test conventions, prefer removing the broad `throws Exception` or narrowing it to the specific exceptions actually thrown.

`resolveHandlers()` creates a new `MetricHandlerHolder` on every refresh cycle. Since `refreshState()` runs repeatedly on a schedule, this causes each handler to be enrolled as “first enrollment” every time, leading to repeated instrument registration and leaking callbacks/instruments (and potentially double-counting metrics). Consider caching/reusing a holder per (MetricDef, handlerName) across refresh cycles (and just updating its `DetectionStatus`), so instruments are created only once.

`MetricExtractor.getStatus()` is now synchronized even though `status` is already `volatile`. This getter is invoked in the metric callback path (`MetricRegistrar.*TypeCallback`), so the added monitor enter/exit can introduce avoidable overhead/lock contention. Consider making `getStatus()` a plain volatile read, and keep synchronization only in `setStatus()` where you need the atomic “check-null then set” logic.

[Best practices] `MetricHandlerHolder` is declared `public` even though it appears to be used only within `io.opentelemetry.instrumentation.jmx.internal.*` packages in this PR. Consider reducing visibility (e.g., package-private) to follow least-access and avoid exposing an internal type unintentionally.

This issue also appears on line 17 of the same file.

[Documentation] The changelog entry mentions only `JmxTelemetry.start()` return type change, but `start(Supplier<...>)` is also changed to return `AutoCloseable`. Consider updating the wording to reflect the full surface area of the breaking change (e.g., “`JmxTelemetry.start*()` methods now return `AutoCloseable`”).

threads.body: `MetricHandlerHolder` is in an `internal` package but is declared `public`, which makes it part of the library's public surface area (even if not intended). Since it appears only used internally, consider making the class package-private (remove `public`) to reduce accidental API exposure. Also consider annotating `getHandler()` with `@Nullable` (or enforcing non-null once set) to reflect the actual nullability contract.

threads.body: This allows specifying both `handler` and `handlers` and does not deduplicate entries, so the same handler name can be added multiple times (e.g., if `handler` is also listed in `handlers`). That can lead to the same handler being enrolled multiple times and potentially producing duplicate instruments/duplicate metric streams. Consider normalizing to a single list (e.g., treat `handler` as a single-element alias), validating non-blank values, and deduplicating while preserving order.

`close()` is not idempotent: if the returned `AutoCloseable` is closed more than once (which is common in defensive cleanup paths), the same instruments may be closed repeatedly, potentially generating warnings or throwing from underlying implementations. Consider clearing `instruments` after closing (or guarding with a `closed` flag) to make shutdown reliable and repeatable.

The parser behavior now depends on the interaction between `mapping` and `handler`/`handlers` (e.g., handler-only rules skip `setMapping`, and empty mapping without handlers is still invalid). There are tests for missing/loaded handlers, but it would be helpful to add coverage for (1) `handlers:` list parsing, (2) a handler-only rule with no mapping, and (3) duplicate handler entries behavior (whether rejected or deduped) to lock in the intended contract.

`enrollHandler()` dereferences `holder.getHandler()` without a null-check, even though `MetricHandlerHolder.getHandler()` is nullable. Currently `BeanFinder` guards this, but the contract isn’t enforced here, so a future call path (or refactor) could trigger an NPE. Consider validating `holder.getHandler()` inside `enrollHandler()` (e.g., early-return with a warning) or making the holder guarantee a non-null handler before enrollment.

This issue also appears on line 246 of the same file.

`shutdown()` ignores the boolean result of `awaitTermination(...)`. If the executor doesn’t terminate within the timeout, the bean-finder thread can keep running and leak resources. Consider checking the return value and logging (or taking additional action) when termination fails.

`MetricHandlerHolder.setHandler()` throws if invoked more than once. Since `BeanFinder` resolves and sets handlers on every `JmxTelemetry.start(...)` call (and `MetricConfiguration`/`MetricDef` instances are reused across starts), calling `start()` a second time on the same `JmxTelemetry` instance will fail with `IllegalStateException`. Consider making handler assignment idempotent (e.g., no-op if already set to the same implementation) or guarding in `BeanFinder` before calling `setHandler()`.

threads.body: `handler.create(...)` is registered without validating the return value. If an SPI implementation mistakenly returns `null`, this will fail later with an unhelpful `NullPointerException` when adding to the `instruments` set or during shutdown. Consider enforcing a non-null `AutoCloseable` (e.g., `requireNonNull` with a clear message, or log+skip when null) to make the SPI contract failure easier to diagnose.
